Family Health

Thyroid cancer: who it affects, the different types and treatment

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Thyroid cancer develops when cells in the thyroid begin to grow abnormally. It is diagnosed more often in women, but it can affect people of any sex and age. Many thyroid cancers respond well to treatment, while some uncommon types need urgent, specialised care. Knowing the exact type matters more than assuming that every thyroid cancer behaves in the same way.

What does the thyroid do?

The thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland at the lower front of the neck. It belongs to the endocrine system, which makes hormones that carry messages around the body. Thyroid hormones influence how the body uses energy, as well as functions such as temperature and heart rate.

Cancer starts when changes within cells allow them to multiply without the usual controls. A growth may remain within the thyroid or spread to nearby structures, lymph nodes or more distant organs. A thyroid cancer that spreads is still named for its thyroid origin.

A thyroid nodule is a lump, not a diagnosis of cancer. Most nodules are benign. Examination and appropriate testing help distinguish common non-cancerous thyroid changes from a tumour that needs treatment.

Is thyroid cancer more common in women?

Yes. The American Cancer Society reports that thyroid cancer occurs almost three times as often in women as in men. The reasons are not fully understood. This difference describes patterns across a population; it cannot determine whether an individual neck lump is cancerous.

Age also affects the pattern of diagnosis, and different cancer types occur at different ages. Having fewer typical risk factors does not mean that symptoms should be ignored. Conversely, belonging to a higher-risk group does not mean that cancer is inevitable.

Claims that thyroid cancer holds a particular worldwide ranking or is the fastest-growing cancer need a date, country and definition. Changes in detection, including finding small tumours during imaging for another reason, can influence recorded incidence. A fixed ranking is less useful than understanding personal findings.

Risk factors: family history, radiation and other influences

A risk factor is associated with a greater chance of developing a disease; it is not proof of what caused it. Relevant factors include a family history of thyroid cancer, certain inherited syndromes, exposure of the thyroid to substantial radiation, and excess body weight. Many people diagnosed with thyroid cancer have no clear explanation for why it developed.

Cowden syndrome, often linked to changes in the PTEN gene, and familial adenomatous polyposis, linked to APC, are examples of inherited conditions associated with some thyroid cancers. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, or MEN2, is particularly relevant to medullary thyroid cancer. A clinician can decide whether a family pattern warrants genetic counselling.

The radiation association is strongest for significant exposure at a young age. Childhood head-and-neck radiotherapy and radioactive fallout are important examples. Historical observations after nuclear disasters, including Chernobyl, and atomic-bomb exposure contributed to understanding this risk.

Radiation dose, age and the body area exposed matter. Routine diagnostic X-rays are not equivalent to high-dose treatment or major fallout exposure. Do not avoid a medically indicated investigation on the assumption that every X-ray creates the same cancer risk; discuss its purpose and alternatives with the clinician.

Broad references to toxins do not identify a particular exposure or establish that it causes thyroid cancer. An exposure history can be discussed during assessment, but an unspecified toxin claim should not lead to detox products or unnecessary testing.

Iodine, diet and inherited risk: avoiding misleading conclusions

The thyroid needs iodine to make hormones, but that does not make iodine supplements a cancer-prevention treatment. Follicular thyroid cancer is more common in iodine-deficient regions, while high iodine intake has also been associated with patterns of papillary cancer. These observations do not establish a safe anticancer dose.

Research on fish, seafood and iodine intake is difficult to separate from wider diet and regional differences. A suggestion of lower risk in a particular study cannot be turned into a promise that eating more seafood will prevent thyroid cancer. Ask for individual advice if you have a diagnosed thyroid condition or a reason to suspect deficiency.

Inherited cancer risk also needs the correct denominator. Around a quarter of medullary thyroid cancers run in families; that is not the same as saying that a fifth or quarter of all thyroid cancers are inherited. Most thyroid cancers are not explained by a known inherited syndrome.

Papillary and follicular thyroid cancers

Papillary cancer is the most common thyroid cancer. It usually grows relatively slowly and often has a favourable outlook. It can spread to lymph nodes in the neck, so a small primary tumour does not remove the need to assess the surrounding area.

Follicular cancer is another differentiated thyroid cancer. Differentiated means that the tumour retains some features of the thyroid cells from which it arose. Follicular cancer can spread through the bloodstream to sites such as the lungs or bones, although many people are diagnosed before that happens.

Both arise from follicular cells, which normally produce thyroid hormone. Their shared origin helps explain why surgery, thyroid-hormone treatment and, in selected cases, radioactive iodine can be useful. The pathology details and extent of disease determine which combination is appropriate.

Oncocytic cancer, previously called Hürthle cell cancer

Oncocytic thyroid carcinoma is the current name commonly used for the cancer previously called Hürthle cell carcinoma. Older material may describe it as a subtype of follicular cancer; current classifications distinguish it as a separate type of differentiated thyroid cancer.

It is uncommon and can behave differently from papillary or follicular cancer. Some tumours are more invasive or less likely to take up radioactive iodine, which can affect treatment planning. The name alone does not tell an individual how aggressive their tumour will be.

The specialist considers features such as invasion, size, spread and the person’s health. A blanket statement that this cancer always has a poor outcome is not accurate. Ask what the pathology report means for the particular case.

Medullary cancer: sporadic and inherited forms

Medullary thyroid cancer starts in C cells, which produce calcitonin. These are different from the follicular cells that make the main thyroid hormones. Because of this difference, investigations, blood markers and treatments are not identical to those used for papillary cancer.

Most medullary cancers are sporadic, meaning they do not arise from an inherited cancer syndrome. A smaller proportion are associated with an inherited RET gene change, sometimes as part of MEN2. Inherited disease can occur in children as well as adults.

People with medullary cancer are usually offered assessment for an inherited RET change. If one is found, relatives may be offered counselling and testing. This is a targeted family assessment, not a recommendation for everyone with a thyroid nodule to buy a genetic test.

For some people with a high-risk inherited RET change, specialists recommend preventive thyroid surgery. Its timing depends on the specific variant and clinical findings. The decision belongs in an experienced endocrine and genetics service.

Anaplastic cancer and thyroid lymphoma

Anaplastic thyroid cancer is rare and often grows rapidly. It needs prompt specialist assessment because it may affect breathing, swallowing or nearby structures. It is classified as stage IV, but that label has substages: it does not mean that every case has already spread to distant organs.

Treatment can involve a combination of approaches, including molecular testing to identify potentially useful targeted medicines. The team also considers symptom relief and protection of the airway. A general description of usually slow-growing thyroid cancer does not apply to this type.

Primary thyroid lymphoma is a different disease involving immune cells in the thyroid. It is associated with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, but lymphoma remains rare and most people with Hashimoto’s do not develop it. A rapidly enlarging thyroid warrants assessment.

Lymphoma treatment commonly involves medicines and sometimes radiotherapy rather than routine removal of the entire thyroid. The lymphoma subtype and extent of disease affect the outlook. It should not be grouped under the same treatment rules as all other thyroid cancers.

Symptoms and the first clinical assessment

A new lump or swelling in the neck is a common reason for investigation. Persistent hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, pressure or neck discomfort can also prompt assessment. These symptoms have many possible causes and do not by themselves establish cancer.

The clinician asks about changes over time, previous radiation treatment, family history and general health, then examines the thyroid and neck lymph nodes. Some cancers are found incidentally during imaging performed for another reason.

Arrange assessment for a persistent or enlarging lump or unexplained voice change. Rapidly increasing swelling, significant difficulty breathing or an inability to swallow safely needs urgent help rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

What blood tests, ultrasound and biopsies can show

Thyroid-function blood tests measure how the gland is working. They can be normal when thyroid cancer is present, so a normal TSH result does not rule it out. Other blood tests, including calcitonin in relevant circumstances, answer different questions.

Ultrasound shows the size and appearance of nodules and neck lymph nodes. It helps determine whether a nodule needs sampling and can guide a fine needle into the appropriate area. Ultrasound findings estimate concern; they are not a substitute for a tissue diagnosis when one is needed.

Fine-needle aspiration removes cells for examination. A core biopsy or a surgical sample may sometimes be needed, depending on the suspected condition or an inconclusive result. Some follicular-pattern tumours require examination of tissue architecture and invasion, which a needle sample alone may not establish.

CT or MRI may help assess structures or disease spread when indicated. A radioactive iodine scan examines iodine uptake and can be useful in selected settings, but it is not a universal screening test or a simple cancer-versus-no-cancer answer. Medullary cancer does not take up iodine in the same way.

A laryngoscopy checks movement of the vocal cords. It may be arranged when voice symptoms or the planned treatment make that information important, including around thyroid surgery.

Surgery or active surveillance: choosing the right extent of care

Surgery is an important treatment for many thyroid cancers. A lobectomy removes one lobe; a total thyroidectomy removes the whole gland. Involved lymph nodes may also need treatment. The choice depends on the tumour type, size, location, spread and the person’s preferences and health.

A single rule that every tumour between one and four centimetres needs the same operation is too broad. The 2025 American Thyroid Association guidance supports lobectomy for many low-risk differentiated cancers, with the decision tailored to specific findings.

For selected very small, low-risk papillary cancers, active surveillance may be an option. This involves planned specialist follow-up and ultrasound, with treatment if defined changes occur. It does not mean leaving a concerning lump unassessed or ignoring symptoms.

Ask about the expected benefit, possible need for further surgery, voice changes, calcium problems and hormone treatment afterward. The team should explain why the proposed approach fits the individual cancer.

Radioactive iodine and external radiation are different treatments

Radioactive iodine is taken by mouth and can be absorbed by iodine-avid thyroid cells. After surgery it may be used to treat selected remaining tissue or cancer. It is useful only when the type of cancer and its risk profile make it appropriate; not everyone with differentiated cancer needs it.

Medullary and anaplastic cancers do not respond to radioactive iodine in the way iodine-avid differentiated cancers can. Oncocytic tumours may also take up less iodine. The specialist explains whether testing or treatment is likely to help.

External-beam radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation, usually X-rays, at a defined area. It is not treatment with ordinary radio waves. It can be considered for selected cancers or disease that cannot be adequately controlled with other approaches.

Preparation, possible side effects and precautions differ between these treatments. Tell the treatment team about pregnancy, pregnancy plans or breastfeeding before radioactive iodine is considered so they can explain the necessary restrictions and timing.

Chemotherapy, targeted medicines and molecular testing

Traditional chemotherapy uses medicines that affect dividing cells. It is not the routine treatment for most early differentiated thyroid cancers, but it may have a role in selected situations, including some anaplastic cancers and lymphomas.

Targeted medicines act on particular growth pathways or molecular changes. Some kinase inhibitors interfere with signals that help a tumour grow or develop a blood supply. Other drugs are selected because testing identifies a specific alteration in the cancer.

These treatments are not automatically needed after every thyroid operation. Their likely benefit, side effects, disease behaviour and alternatives must be weighed together. Advanced or uncommon cancers may also warrant discussion of an appropriate clinical trial.

Thyroid hormone and follow-up after treatment

After the whole thyroid is removed, lifelong thyroid-hormone replacement is needed. Some people also need replacement after removal of one lobe. Levothyroxine restores a hormone the body needs; its dose is adjusted using blood tests and clinical assessment.

For selected differentiated cancers, treatment may also aim to lower TSH to reduce stimulation of thyroid cells. The target depends on risk and response to treatment. Strong TSH suppression is not appropriate for everyone and does not guarantee that cancer cannot return.

Follow-up may include examination, neck ultrasound and type-specific blood markers. For example, thyroglobulin can be useful in certain differentiated-cancer follow-up settings, while medullary cancer is monitored differently. Results need interpretation in light of the operation and other treatment received.

Tell the team about persistent voice problems, symptoms suggesting low calcium, difficulties taking hormone tablets or other treatment effects. Cancer can recur after an initially successful treatment, so keep the agreed follow-up even when you feel well.

Understanding survival figures and prevention

Outlook varies greatly by cancer type and stage. Small differentiated cancers often have a very favourable prognosis, while aggressive or widely spread cancers require a different discussion. Age, tumour features, treatment response and overall health also matter.

For context, current US SEER data report five-year relative survival of 98.3% for thyroid cancer overall, based on diagnoses in 2016–2022. This population measure accounts for deaths from other causes; it is not an individual prediction, a cure rate or a promise that every subtype has the same outlook.

There is no guaranteed way to prevent most thyroid cancers. Appropriate medical imaging decisions and management of known inherited risk are more useful than unsupported supplements or detox plans. People with relevant family histories can ask whether genetic counselling would change their care.

A useful next conversation focuses on the exact diagnosis: what type is it, how far has it spread, what are the treatment choices, and what follow-up will be needed? Those answers make general cancer information meaningful for an individual.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Specialist and cancer-agency resources distinguish differentiated, medullary and anaplastic cancers; primary thyroid lymphoma needs a separate treatment approach. Normal thyroid-function blood tests do not exclude a thyroid cancer.

Recent ATA guidance supports risk-based decisions about the extent of surgery and selected active surveillance. Overall survival statistics cannot replace a discussion of the individual pathology and stage.

How BeMama can help

Keep the pathology name, planned investigations and questions for the specialist together. Recording what the team has confirmed can make it easier to discuss care with family without treating every thyroid condition as the same disease.

When to seek help

A persistent neck lump or voice change needs clinical assessment. Rapid swelling or breathing difficulty needs urgent help. Do not start iodine supplements, change hormone treatment or delay investigations on the basis of a general article.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Thyroid cancer is diagnosed more often in women, but can affect anyone.
  • Most thyroid nodules are not cancer.
  • The precise cancer type determines treatment and follow-up.
  • Normal thyroid-function tests do not rule out cancer.
  • Some low-risk cancers can be monitored or treated with a smaller operation.
  • Survival percentages describe groups, not an individual outcome.

Frequently asked questions

Is thyroid cancer more common in women or men?

It is diagnosed almost three times as often in women, according to the American Cancer Society. A concerning lump still needs assessment regardless of sex.

Can thyroid cancer occur with a normal TSH result?

Yes. Thyroid-function blood tests can be normal. Ultrasound and, when indicated, a biopsy investigate the nodule itself.

Does having a thyroid nodule mean I have cancer?

No. Most nodules are benign. The clinician uses the history, examination and test results to decide what follow-up is appropriate.

Are Hürthle cell and oncocytic cancer the same term?

Oncocytic thyroid carcinoma is the current name commonly used for what was previously called Hürthle cell carcinoma.

Is a quarter of all thyroid cancer inherited?

No. The roughly one-quarter figure applies to medullary thyroid cancer, a small subset, rather than all thyroid cancers.

Must the entire thyroid always be removed?

No. Some cancers are suitable for lobectomy, and selected very small, low-risk papillary cancers may be monitored. A specialist determines whether those options fit.

Does every thyroid cancer respond to radioactive iodine?

No. Treatment depends on iodine uptake, cancer type and risk. Medullary and anaplastic cancers are not treated this way.

Does stage IV anaplastic cancer always mean distant spread?

No. All anaplastic thyroid cancers use stage IV categories, but their substages distinguish disease confined to the thyroid, nearby spread and distant spread.

Will I need thyroid hormone forever?

After total thyroid removal, yes. Some people also need it after a lobectomy. The dose and TSH target are individualised.

Can iodine or seafood prevent thyroid cancer?

There is no established iodine-supplement or seafood regimen that guarantees prevention. Excess iodine can also cause problems, so seek advice before supplementing for a thyroid concern.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
